Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say
article.full_text: Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week. The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict. The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe. Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict. One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat. They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted. The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience. A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy. Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict. The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month. One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa. The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning. Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”. One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline. The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US. “Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. article.title: Kemi Badenoch condemns Reform UK’s ‘authoritarian’ press bans
article.full_text: Reform UK’s decision to ban some journalists from its conference shows that Nigel Farage would use state power to target opponents and be authoritarian in government, Kemi Badenoch has said. Answering questions after a speech on defence in London, the Conservative leader was asked about Reform’s decision to refuse accreditation to a series of journalists for its conference this week. One of the journalists was Anna Isaac, the Guardian’s City editor, who broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Farage’s attacks on the media were “very personal” at times, Badenoch said, also citing the targeting of journalists by Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson. She continued: “I think you could … [see] what kind of government they would be – authoritarian and using state power actually to pursue opponents is what they’ve effectively been threatening. “We believe in free speech. We believe in a free press. And yes, of course, that might be painful for us as politicians, but public scrutiny is part of the gig. If Nigel Farage can’t handle difficult questions about his dodgy £5m then he shouldn’t be a politician.” Reform refused to say why it had banned Isaac. In other questions at the event, Badenoch defended her party’s new policy of cutting housing benefit as a way to finance increased defence spending, but declined to say if any savings might be cancelled out by other costs, for example by people being made homeless. In an announcement overnight, the Conservatives said they would make defence spending hit 3% of GDP by 2029-30 through £10bn of savings, primarily from social security. A significant chunk of this would be made by cutting local housing allowances, which sets out how much housing benefit people receive in their local area for private tenancies. This has been frozen anyway since 2024, and already does not fully cover the majority of rents. Asked whether the assumed savings factored in likely knock-on costs, for example people losing their homes and having to seek emergency accommodation from councils, Badenoch slightly evaded the question. “It all needs to be coordinated,” she said. “What we are doing on defence is very closely linked to welfare. My shadow welfare secretary, Helen Whately, is looking at all of the impacts across the board, because we know that every change does create a new situation.” Badenoch stressed what she said was the urgent need for increased defence spending given the threat from Russia, saying that other European countries like Poland and Germany were moving more quickly. She said: “Like Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass. I cannot tell you how urgent this is.” Burnham’s government has pledged to meet a Nato commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, but has delayed giving a timing for reaching 3% of GDP. As Starmer’s defence secretary, John Healey insisted this should be reached by 2030, but has dropped the target as Burnham’s chancellor. Separately, Badenoch rejected concerns that her policy to bar non-UK nationals from social housing could see a repeat of the Windrush scandal, where checks on immigration status saw people who had lived their lives in the UK denied access to services. She said: “I don’t think that this is anything like what happened with Windrush, where there were people who had citizenship but couldn’t prove it. And there are lessons that have been learned around the administration of those schemes.”
